title: Pictographs, Bar Graphs and Pie Charts
seo_title: Grade 4 Pictographs, Bar Graphs and Pie Charts Worksheets with Answers (CAPS Maths)
short_title: Pictographs, Bar Graphs and Pie Charts
standard_code: Grade 4: 5.2 Representing data; 5.3 Analysing, interpreting and reporting data
standard_text: Draw a variety of graphs to display and interpret data, including pictographs and bar graphs; critically read and interpret data represented in words, pictographs, bar graphs and pie charts; analyse data by answering questions related to data categories and report on the data.
meta_desc: Free CAPS Grade 4 data handling worksheets: pictographs with keys, bar graphs, comparing data, two-step questions and pie charts. 100 questions with memos.
key_big: Read the key or the scale first.
key_sub: A pie chart shows parts of a whole.
body_html:
How to think about it

  • A pictograph uses pictures. Read the key: one picture may stand for 2, 5 or 10.
  • A bar graph uses bars. Read the scale on the side and the top of each bar.
  • A pie chart shows parts of a whole: half the circle is half of the data.
  • Answer questions, compare categories and write a short summary of what the graph shows.

Examples

Example

Key: one picture = 5 learners; 4 pictures

4 × 5

Answer: 20 learners

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
Forgetting the keyMultiply by what one picture stands for.
Between grid linesHalfway between 10 and 20 is 15.
Pie part as a numberA quarter of 40 learners is 10.

items.e: Look at the key: each star stands for 2 shells. The Ethan row has 5 stars and half a star: 5 × 2 = 10, and half of 2 is 1, so 10 + 1 = 11 shells.

items.q: In this pictograph, what does half a square stand for?
items.e: The key says one whole square = 2 books. Half a square is half of 2, which is 1 book. (Half a symbol is not always 1: it is half of the key.)
Look at the key: each star stands for 2 learners. AFL: 8 × 2 = 16 and Swimming: 6 × 2 = 12. How many more means find the difference: 16 − 12 = 4 learners.

items.q: Which row shows 5 votes?
items.e: Half a square is 1, so 5 votes is 2 and a half squares. The Orange row has 2 squares and half a square: 2 × 2 = 4, and half of 2 is 1, so 4 + 1 = 5 votes.

items.q: Each star stands for 5 votes. Netball got 40 votes. How many stars should be in the Netball row?
items.e: Count in 5s until you reach 40: 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35, 40. That is 8 steps, so draw 8 stars. Check: 8 × 5 = 40. (Drawing 40 stars would mean each star stands for 1.)

items.q: Which row shows the fewest cans?

items.q: Each circle stands for 10 learners. 45 learners ride a bike to school. What should the Bike row show?
items.e: 45 = 40 + 5. 40 is 4 circles (4 × 10 = 40). 5 is half of 10, so add half a circle. Draw 4 and a half circles. (Drawing 45 circles would mean each circle stands for 1.)
